No new package today, no new geometry or verb to learn. This far in,
it's time to build the thing the whole scenario has been pointing at
since chapter 0: **the one-page Situation Brief** the Commissioner reads
before the incident-command call. Everything you've made so far — the
cleaned table, the trend chart, the statewide map — was an ingredient.
Today you plate them into a single document a person outside R can open
and act on.

## The arc so far

| Part | Question it answered | What it left in `covid-briefing/` |
|---|---|---|
| 00 — Orientation | Why R, and how is the project folder organized? | The scaffold itself, and `data/raw/` with the CT COVID CSV |
| 01 — Working with Real Data | How do I read, inspect, and trust this file? | A Hartford-only tibble, filtered and column-renamed by hand |
| 02 — Cleaning Data | How do I fix names, dates, and messy text? | `covid_clean` — every column name fixed, dates parsed, town names trimmed and title-cased |
| 03 — Data Visualization | How do I show this to someone who won't open a CSV? | A trend chart and a statewide map, saved to `outputs/figures/` |

Each chapter's project picked up exactly where the last one left off.
That's on purpose — a real analysis rarely restarts from scratch every
time a new technique gets introduced.

## This week's briefing summary

A brief is not a pile of numbers — it opens with the answer. The
Commissioner's standing question since chapter 0 was *is it getting worse
in Hartford?*, so the brief leads with a one-line verdict and then backs
it with the figures. Build that verdict the same way you'd build any
finding: `dplyr` to pull the numbers, `lubridate` to decide which date
counts as "now", and `glue` to turn it into a sentence a person can read.

```{r}
#| label: status-setup
#| include: false
covid_data <- read_book_data("ct-covid-by-town-2026-06-30.csv")

covid_clean <-
  covid_data |>
  clean_names() |>
  mutate(last_update_date = mdy(last_update_date)) |>
  arrange(town, last_update_date) |>
  group_by(town) |>
  mutate(new_cases = total_cases - lag(total_cases)) |>
  ungroup()
```

```{r}
#| label: status-numbers
latest_date <- max(covid_clean$last_update_date)
days_of_data <- as.numeric(latest_date - min(covid_clean$last_update_date))

statewide_latest <-
  covid_clean |>
  filter(last_update_date == latest_date) |>
  summarise(
    total_cases = sum(total_cases, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_deaths = sum(total_deaths, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

hartford_latest <-
  covid_clean |>
  filter(town == "Hartford", last_update_date == latest_date) |>
  select(total_cases, total_deaths)
```

The verdict is a comparison: Hartford's most recent week of reports
against the week before it. Averaging over a week smooths out the
reporting noise you met back in chapter 1 — a single low weekend or a
one-day correction won't flip the answer on its own.

```{r}
#| label: status-finding
# Hartford's daily new-case series, oldest report to newest.
hartford_series <-
  covid_clean |>
  filter(town == "Hartford", !is.na(new_cases)) |>
  arrange(last_update_date)

# Most recent 7 reports vs. the 7 before them.
recent_new <- tail(hartford_series$new_cases, 14)
prior_avg <- mean(head(recent_new, 7))
latest_avg <- mean(tail(recent_new, 7))

verdict <- if (latest_avg > prior_avg) {
  "getting worse"
} else {
  "holding steady or improving"
}

verdict
```

```{r}
#| label: status-summary
briefing_summary <- glue(
  "Bottom line: Hartford is {verdict}. Daily new cases there averaged ",
  "{round(latest_avg, 1)} over the last week of reports, against ",
  "{round(prior_avg, 1)} the week before.\n\n",
  "Status as of {latest_date} ({days_of_data} days of data collected):\n",
  "Statewide: {format(statewide_latest$total_cases, big.mark = ',')} total cases, ",
  "{format(statewide_latest$total_deaths, big.mark = ',')} total deaths.\n",
  "Hartford: {format(hartford_latest$total_cases, big.mark = ',')} total cases, ",
  "{format(hartford_latest$total_deaths, big.mark = ',')} total deaths."
)

briefing_summary
```

A verdict on top, the supporting numbers underneath, and every value
computed — correct as of whatever the latest date in the file happens to
be, not typed in by hand. That's the difference between a query result
and a briefing: it opens with the answer.

## Assembling the one-page brief

The verdict paragraph is the words. Chapter 3 already saved the pictures
to `outputs/figures/`. A briefing is those two things on one page, with a
title and an "as of" date, rendered to something you can email or print.

That page is its own small Quarto document. Create
`docs/situation-brief.qmd` in your project and give it this:

````{verbatim}
#| lang: markdown
---
title: "COVID-19 Situation Brief"
format: html
---

```{r}
#| label: brief-setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(here)
library(glue)

# Read the clean table chapter 2 saved — no re-cleaning needed.
covid_clean <- read_csv(here("data", "processed", "covid_clean.csv"))

latest_date <- max(covid_clean$last_update_date)

hartford_series <-
  covid_clean |>
  filter(town == "Hartford", !is.na(new_cases)) |>
  arrange(last_update_date)

recent_new <- tail(hartford_series$new_cases, 14)
prior_avg  <- mean(head(recent_new, 7))
latest_avg <- mean(tail(recent_new, 7))
verdict <- if (latest_avg > prior_avg) "getting worse" else "holding steady or improving"
```

**As of `r latest_date`.** Prepared for the Commissioner ahead of the
incident-command call.

## Bottom line

`r glue("Hartford is **{verdict}** — daily new cases averaged {round(latest_avg, 1)} over the last week of reports, against {round(prior_avg, 1)} the week before.")`

## Hartford vs. the statewide average

![](../outputs/figures/hartford_vs_state_trend.png)

## Statewide test positivity

![](../outputs/figures/statewide_positivity_map.png)
````

Then render it — from the R console, or the Render button in your IDE:

```{r}
#| eval: false
quarto::quarto_render(here("docs", "situation-brief.qmd"))
```

That drops `docs/situation-brief.html` in your project: **one page, the
verdict up top, both figures underneath, dated automatically.** That —
not a tibble, not a lone PNG — is what the scenario has meant by "a
briefing for the Commissioner" all along. This is the checkpoint's
deliverable, and the first artifact in the book a non-R person could open
and use without you standing next to them.

::: {.callout-note}
The brief reads `data/processed/covid_clean.csv` (chapter 2's saved
table) and embeds the two figures from `outputs/figures/` (chapter 3's
`ggsave()` calls). If you skipped either save, run it now — the brief has
nothing to assemble without them. That dependency is the whole point:
clean once, chart once, and the brief is just composition.
:::

## What your project folder should look like now

```{r}
#| eval: false
fs::dir_tree(here::here(), recurse = 2)
```

If you've been following along in your own `covid-briefing/` project,
you should see something close to this:

```
covid-briefing/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   │   └── ct_covid_by_town_2026-06-30.csv
│   └── processed/
│       └── covid_clean.csv        # if you uncommented the write_csv() in ch. 2
├── R/
├── scripts/
├── outputs/
│   ├── figures/
│   │   ├── hartford_new_cases.png
│   │   ├── hartford_vs_state_trend.png
│   │   └── statewide_positivity_map.png
│   └── tables/
└── docs/
    ├── situation-brief.qmd
    └── situation-brief.html        # the one-page brief, rendered
```

If your folder looks different, that's fine — the point isn't to match
this tree exactly, it's to notice that the folder is *filling up with
real artifacts* instead of staying empty. That's what progress looks
like in a data project: not lines of code, but files someone else could
open and use.

## What's still manual

Being honest about the current state of things:

- Every chapter's project re-runs the cleaning steps by hand, from the
  top, in a `.qmd` file. Nothing here is a function you could call
  twice.
- The brief looks self-updating — its date and verdict are computed —
  but it's only as fresh as the CSV underneath it. That CSV is a
  snapshot someone downloaded by hand. Nothing fetches new data
  automatically, so "this week's brief" still means someone
  re-downloading and re-rendering every week.
- "Hartford" is typed directly into the code. Asking the brief about a
  different town means editing the file, not passing an argument.
- There's no history of any of this yet — if you overwrite a file by
  accident, it's just gone.

None of that is a problem yet — it's normal for a project this size.
It becomes a problem the day someone asks for the same briefing next
week, for a different town, without you sitting at the keyboard.

## What's next

The parts ahead exist to close exactly those gaps:

- **Managing Code** — version control, so every change to this
  project is recorded, reversible, and explainable to someone other
  than you.
- **Intermediate R: Automating the Manual Steps** — turning repeated
  code into functions, and pulling fresh data straight from the state's
  API instead of re-downloading a CSV by hand.

The scenario hasn't changed: the Commissioner still wants to know if
it's getting worse in Hartford. What changes from here is how much of
the answer you have to rebuild yourself every time someone asks.
